edges.effect_quant: Across meta-analyses of observational studies, ever use of oral contraceptives is usually associated with roughly 15% to 20% lower colorectal-cancer risk.
edges.mechanism: Combined oral contraceptives alter estrogen and progestin exposure in ways that may affect bile-acid metabolism, colonic epithelial turnover, and insulin-related growth signaling. Whatever benefit exists appears modest and long-lagged rather than a strong near-term pharmacologic protection effect.
edges.summary: This is one of the more consistent cancer associations in the hormonal-contraception literature. Multiple meta-analyses have found lower colorectal-cancer risk in ever-users versus never-users, and the signal has remained visible across both cohort and case-control data even though the exact magnitude varies.
edges.caveats: The entire evidence base is observational, so screening behavior, parity, and other reproductive-pattern differences could still influence the estimate. This edge should not be read as a reason to prescribe oral contraceptives for cancer prevention by themselves.
